mk: The shortest and, on most scholars' view, the earliest Gospel, written around 70 CE. Mark's Greek is plain and fast: sentences strung together with {mk 1:12 Καὶ εὐθὺς} (“and immediately”), and vivid present tenses. It opens without a birth story, {mk 1:1 Ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ} (“the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ”); the SBLGNT omits “Son of God” here, following some early manuscripts. Mark's Jesus is urgent and secretive, his disciples persistently fail to understand, and the oldest manuscripts end at the empty tomb in fear. The vocabulary below shows the texture: *euthys*, unclean spirits, the sea, Jesus “looking around”.
mt: Matthew rewrites about 90% of Mark and adds a large body of teaching, gathered into five great discourses. Many readers see a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses. It begins with a genealogy, {mt 1:1 Βίβλος γενέσεως} (“the book of the genesis”), echoing Genesis itself, and keeps showing scripture fulfilled. Its Jesus comes {mt 5:17 οὐκ ἦλθον καταλῦσαι ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι} (“not to abolish but to fulfill”) the Law, and its closing promise, “I am with you always”, answers the Emmanuel of its first chapter, {mt 1:23 Μεθ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός} (“God with us”). The vocabulary below shows Matthew's habits: *tote* (“then”), “the kingdom of **heaven**”, hypocrites, and the formal “came to him”.
lk: The only evangelist who explains his method, Luke writes in polished Greek for a patron, {lk 1:3 κράτιστε Θεόφιλε} (“most excellent Theophilus”), promising an account written {lk 1:3 ἀκριβῶς καθεξῆς} (“carefully, in order”). His Gospel is the first volume of a two-part work that continues in Acts. It is shaped by a journey toward Jerusalem, a word near the top of his vocabulary list, and by concern for the poor, women, Samaritans and sinners: {lk 19:10 ἦλθεν γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ζητῆσαι καὶ σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός} (“the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost”). Many of the best-loved parables, including the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, appear only in Luke.
jn: John is the Gospel that stands apart. It opens before creation, {jn 1:1 Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος} (“in the beginning was the Word”), and announces that {jn 1:14 ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο} (“the Word became flesh”). John has few parables and no exorcisms. In their place are long discourses, seven “signs”, and “I am” sayings, which is why *egō* (“I”) sits near the top of its vocabulary list, alongside “world”, “believe”, “Father”, “testify” and “remain”. It shares relatively little wording with the Synoptics, as this site's map shows, and it explains its own purpose: {jn 20:31 ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται ἵνα πιστεύητε} (“these things are written so that you may believe”).
